In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''Quot scheme''' is a scheme parametrizing sheaves on a [[projective scheme]]. More specifically, if ''X'' is a projective scheme over a Noetherian scheme ''S'' and if ''F'' is a [[coherent sheaf]] on ''X'', then there is a scheme <math>\operatorname{Quot}_F(X)</math> whose set of [[functor of points|''T''-points]] <math>\operatorname{Quot}_F(X)(T) = \operatorname{Mor}_S(T, \operatorname{Quot}_F(X))</math> is the set of isomorphism classes of the [[quotient by an equivalence relation|quotients]] of <math>F \times_S T</math> that are flat over ''T''. The notion was introduced by [[Alexander Grothendieck]].<ref>Grothendieck, Alexander. [http://www.numdam.org/item/?id=SB_1960-1961__6__249_0  Techniques de construction et théorèmes d'existence en géométrie algébrique IV : les schémas de Hilbert.]  Séminaire Bourbaki : années 1960/61, exposés 205-222, Séminaire Bourbaki, no. 6 (1961), Talk no. 221, p. 249-276</ref>

It is typically used to construct another scheme parametrizing geometric objects that are of interest such as a [[Hilbert scheme]]. (In fact, taking ''F'' to be the structure sheaf <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math> gives a Hilbert scheme.)

== Definition ==
For a [[scheme of finite type]] <math>X \to S</math> over a [[Noetherian scheme|Noetherian]] base scheme <math>S</math>, and a [[coherent sheaf]] <math>\mathcal{E} \in \text{Coh}(X)</math>, there is a functor<ref>{{cite book
| last=Nitsure | first=Nitin
| date=2005
| chapter=Construction of Hilbert and Quot Schemes
| arxiv=math/0504590
| title=Fundamental algebraic geometry: Grothendieck’s FGA explained
| series=Mathematical Surveys and Monographs
| volume=123
| publisher=American Mathematical Society
| isbn=978-0-8218-4245-4
| pages=105–137}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1= Altman|first1=Allen B. |last2=Kleiman |first2=Steven L. |date=1980 |title=Compactifying the Picard scheme |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=50–112 |doi=10.1016/0001-8708(80)90043-2 |doi-access=free |issn=0001-8708}}</ref><blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}: (Sch/S)^{op} \to \text{Sets}</math></blockquote>sending <math>T \to S</math> to<blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}(T) = \left\{
(\mathcal{F}, q) : \begin{matrix}
    \mathcal{F}\in \text{QCoh}(X_T) \\
    \mathcal{F}\ \text{finitely presented over}\ X_T \\
    \text{Supp}(\mathcal{F}) \text{ is proper over } T \\
    \mathcal{F} \text{ is flat over } T \\
    q: \mathcal{E}_T \to \mathcal{F} \text{ surjective}
\end{matrix}
\right\}/ \sim</math></blockquote>where <math>X_T = X\times_ST</math> and <math>\mathcal{E}_T = pr_X^*\mathcal{E}</math> under the projection <math>pr_X: X_T \to X</math>. There is an [[equivalence relation]] given by <math>(\mathcal{F},q) \sim (\mathcal{F}',q')</math> if there is an isomorphism <math>\mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F}'</math> commuting with the two projections <math>q, q'</math>; that is,<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
\mathcal{E}_T & \xrightarrow{q} & \mathcal{F} \\
\downarrow{} & & \downarrow \\
\mathcal{E}_T & \xrightarrow{q'} & \mathcal{F}'
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>is a [[commutative diagram]] for <math>\mathcal{E}_T \xrightarrow{id} \mathcal{E}_T</math> . Alternatively, there is an equivalent condition of holding <math>\text{ker}(q) = \text{ker}(q')</math>. This is called the '''quot functor''' which has a natural stratification into a disjoint union of subfunctors, each of which is represented by a projective <math>S</math>-scheme called the '''quot scheme''' associated to a Hilbert polynomial <math>\Phi</math>.

=== Hilbert polynomial ===
For a relatively [[ample line bundle|very ample]] [[line bundle]] <math>\mathcal{L} \in \text{Pic}(X)</math><ref>Meaning a basis <math>s_i</math> for the global sections <math>\Gamma(X,\mathcal{L})</math> defines an embedding <math>\mathbb{s}:X \to \mathbb{P}^N_S</math> for <math>N = \text{dim}(\Gamma(X,\mathcal{L}))</math></ref> and any [[closed point]] <math>s \in S</math> there is a function <math>\Phi_\mathcal{F}: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}</math> sending

<math>m \mapsto \chi(\mathcal{F}_s(m)) = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i\text{dim}_{\kappa(s)}H^i(X,\mathcal{F}_s\otimes \mathcal{L}_s^{\otimes m})</math>

which is a polynomial for <math>m >> 0</math>. This is called the [[Hilbert polynomial]] which gives a natural stratification of the quot functor. Again, for <math>\mathcal{L}</math> fixed there is a disjoint union of subfunctors<blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S} = \coprod_{\Phi \in \mathbb{Q}[t]} \mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}^{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}</math></blockquote>where<blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}^{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}(T) = \left\{ (\mathcal{F},q) \in \mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}(T) : \Phi_\mathcal{F} = \Phi \right\}</math></blockquote>The Hilbert polynomial <math>\Phi_\mathcal{F}</math> is the Hilbert polynomial of <math>\mathcal{F}_t</math> for closed points <math>t \in T</math>. Note the Hilbert polynomial is independent of the choice of very ample line bundle <math>\mathcal{L}</math>.

=== Grothendieck's existence theorem ===
It is a theorem of Grothendieck's that the functors <math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}^{\Phi,\mathcal{L}}</math> are all representable by projective schemes <math>\text{Quot}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}^{\Phi}</math> over <math>S</math>.

== Examples ==

=== Grassmannian ===
The [[Grassmannian]] <math>G(n,k)</math> of <math>k</math>-planes in an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[vector space]] has a universal quotient<blockquote><math>\mathcal{O}_{G(n,k)}^{\oplus k} \to \mathcal{U}</math></blockquote>where <math>\mathcal{U}_x</math> is the <math>k</math>-plane represented by <math>x \in G(n,k)</math>. Since <math>\mathcal{U}</math> is locally free and at every point it represents a <math>k</math>-plane, it has the constant Hilbert polynomial <math>\Phi(\lambda) = k</math>. This shows <math>G(n,k)</math> represents the quot functor<blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{O}_{G(n,k)}^{\oplus(n)}/\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})/\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})}^{k,\mathcal{O}_{G(n,k)}}</math></blockquote>

==== Projective space ====
As a special case, we can construct the projective bundle <math>\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})</math> over <math>X</math> as the quot scheme<blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}^{1,\mathcal{O}_X}_{\mathcal{E}/X/S}</math></blockquote>for a sheaf <math>\mathcal{E}</math> on an <math>S</math>-scheme <math>X</math>.

=== Hilbert scheme ===
The Hilbert scheme is a special example of the quot scheme. Notice a subscheme <math>Z \subset X</math> can be given as a projection<blockquote><math>\mathcal{O}_X \to \mathcal{O}_Z</math></blockquote>and a flat family of such projections parametrized by a scheme <math>T \in Sch/S</math> can be given by<blockquote><math>\mathcal{O}_{X_T} \to \mathcal{F}</math></blockquote>Since there is a hilbert polynomial associated to <math>Z</math>, denoted <math>\Phi_Z</math>, there is an isomorphism of schemes<blockquote><math>\text{Quot}_{\mathcal{O}_X/X/S}^{\Phi_Z} \cong \text{Hilb}_{X/S}^{\Phi_Z}</math></blockquote>

==== Example of a parameterization ====
If <math>X = \mathbb{P}^n_{k}</math> and <math>S = \text{Spec}(k)</math> for an [[algebraically closed field]], then a non-zero section <math>s \in \Gamma(\mathcal{O}(d))</math> has vanishing locus <math>Z = Z(s)</math> with Hilbert polynomial<blockquote><math>\Phi_Z(\lambda) = \binom{n+\lambda}{n} - \binom{n-d+\lambda}{n}</math></blockquote>Then, there is a surjection<blockquote><math>\mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{O}_Z</math></blockquote>with kernel <math>\mathcal{O}(-d)</math>. Since <math>s</math> was an arbitrary non-zero section, and the vanishing locus of <math>a\cdot s</math> for <math>a \in k^*</math> gives the same vanishing locus, the scheme <math>Q=\mathbb{P}(\Gamma(\mathcal{O}(d)))</math> gives a natural parameterization of all such sections. There is a sheaf <math>\mathcal{E}</math> on <math>X\times Q</math> such that for any <math>[s] \in Q</math>, there is an associated subscheme <math>Z \subset X</math> and surjection <math>\mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{O}_Z</math>. This construction represents the quot functor<blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{O}/\mathbb{P}^n/\text{Spec}(k)}^{\Phi_Z}</math></blockquote>

==== Quadrics in the projective plane ====
If <math>X = \mathbb{P}^2</math> and <math>s \in \Gamma(\mathcal{O}(2))</math>, the Hilbert polynomial is<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\Phi_Z(\lambda) &= \binom{2 + \lambda}{2} - \binom{2 - 2 + \lambda}{2} \\
&= \frac{(\lambda + 2)(\lambda + 1)}{2} - \frac{\lambda(\lambda - 1)}{2} \\
&= \frac{\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2}{2} - \frac{\lambda^2 - \lambda}{2} \\
&= \frac{2\lambda + 2}{2} \\
&= \lambda + 1
\end{align}</math></blockquote>and<blockquote><math>\text{Quot}_{\mathcal{O}/\mathbb{P}^2/\text{Spec}(k)}^{\lambda + 1} \cong \mathbb{P}(\Gamma(\mathcal{O}(2))) \cong \mathbb{P}^{5}</math></blockquote>The universal quotient over <math>\mathbb{P}^5\times\mathbb{P}^2</math> is given by<blockquote><math>\mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{U}</math></blockquote>where the fiber over a point <math>[Z] \in \text{Quot}_{\mathcal{O}/\mathbb{P}^2/\text{Spec}(k)}^{\lambda + 1}</math> gives the projective morphism<blockquote><math>\mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{O}_Z</math></blockquote>For example, if <math>[Z] = [a_{0}:a_{1}:a_{2}:a_{3}:a_{4}:a_{5}]</math> represents the coefficients of <blockquote><math>f = a_0x^2 + a_1xy + a_2xz + a_3y^2 + a_4yz + a_5z^2</math></blockquote>then the universal quotient over <math>[Z]</math> gives the short [[exact sequence]]<blockquote><math>0 \to \mathcal{O}(-2)\xrightarrow{f}\mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{O}_Z \to 0</math></blockquote>

=== Semistable vector bundles on a curve ===
[[Semistable vector bundle]]s on a curve <math>C</math> of genus <math>g</math> can equivalently be described as locally free sheaves of finite rank. Such locally free sheaves <math>\mathcal{F}</math> of rank <math>n</math> and degree <math>d</math> have the properties<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://userpage.fu-berlin.de/hoskins/M15_Lecture_notes.pdf|title=Moduli Problems and Geometric Invariant Theory|last=Hoskins|first=Victoria|date=|website=|pages=68, 74–85|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200301001913/https://userpage.fu-berlin.de/hoskins/M15_Lecture_notes.pdf|archive-date=1 March 2020|access-date=}}</ref>

# <math>H^1(C,\mathcal{F}) = 0</math>
# <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is generated by global sections

for <math>d > n(2g-1)</math>. This implies there is a surjection<blockquote><math>H^0(C,\mathcal{F})\otimes \mathcal{O}_C \cong \mathcal{O}_C^{\oplus N} \to \mathcal{F}</math></blockquote>Then, the quot scheme <math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{O}_C^{\oplus N}/\mathcal{C}/\mathbb{Z}}</math> parametrizes all such surjections. Using the [[Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem]] the dimension <math>N</math> is equal to<blockquote><math>\chi(\mathcal{F}) = d + n(1-g)</math></blockquote>For a fixed line bundle <math>\mathcal{L}</math> of degree <math>1</math> there is a twisting <math>\mathcal{F}(m) = \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes m}</math>, shifting the degree by <math>nm</math>, so<blockquote><math>\chi(\mathcal{F}(m)) = mn + d + n(1-g)</math><ref name=":0" /></blockquote>giving the Hilbert polynomial<blockquote><math>\Phi_\mathcal{F}(\lambda) = n\lambda + d + n(1-g)</math></blockquote>Then, the locus of semi-stable vector bundles is contained in<blockquote><math>\mathcal{Quot}_{\mathcal{O}_C^{\oplus N}/\mathcal{C}/\mathbb{Z}}^{\Phi_\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{L}}</math></blockquote>which can be used to construct the moduli space <math>\mathcal{M}_C(n,d)</math> of semistable vector bundles using a [[GIT quotient]].<ref name=":0" />
